title: RBA 'caught off guard' by inflation
full_text:
Former Reserve Bank of Australia board member Ian Harper acknowledged the RBA was caught off-guard by the resurgence in inflation last year because it assumed the Australian economy could sustain more demand without generating price pressures.
Harper also said the central bank could raise interest rates again before the end of the year and was starting to give more weight to short-term inflation expectations in its cash rate decisions, a shift from its traditional approach.
That shift, from looking through temporary swings while longer-term expectations remain anchored, could make the central bank more willing to respond to inflation shocks, raising the risk of a fifth rate increase this year as it tries to stop new price pressures becoming embedded.
"The expectation that demand wouldn't recover as rapidly as it did was underestimated, and secondly ... the bank was still operating off an assumption of productivity growth of 1.2 per cent to around 2 per cent," Harper said at an event in Sydney hosted by the Centre for Independent Studies.
"Productivity growth was weaker than expected. Demand growth was stronger than expected. Now that's before you start talking about oil prices."
Last week the nine-member monetary policy board unanimously agreed to raise the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent as governor Michele Bullock warned the central bank would lift interest rates again if needed to prevent high inflation becoming embedded.
Money markets predict a 34 per cent chance the RBA will raise the cash rate for the fifth time this year at its next meeting in November. In a statement explaining its decision to raise the cash rate by 0.25 per centage points last week, the RBA board acknowledged that "[short]-term measures of inflation expectations remain elevated".
Harper told the CIS event that those short-term measures were becoming more important as policymakers reconsidered whether they could still safely treat them as temporary noise, even as long-term expectations remain around the midpoint of the central bank's 2 to 3 per cent target range.
"As the bank says from time-to-time, long-term inflation expectations over a 10-year horizon remain anchored. In my era of economics, that was always a huge sigh of relief," Harper said.
